articles.title: How to Scrape Funda Property Listings in Python with Funda Scraper
articles.description: By the end of this tutorial you will have a Python script that pulls Dutch homes for sale or for rent from funda.nl into structured rows: asking price, address, living area, rooms, bedrooms, energy label, agency and photo links. Funda is a Dutch property portal, and its search pages are not friendly to a quick requests script. In my tests on 7 November 2026, plain HTTP clients got an "Access Denied" stub or a verification page instead of results. Funda Scraper (reventadata/funda-scraper) is the Apify Actor I built to deal with that. You send it a search, it returns one row per listing. This guide runs it from Python with the Apify API client, and the sample rows below come from a real capture of a Utrecht rental search, not from an invented example. Prerequisites You need three things: Python 3.11 or newer (the Apify client for Python 3.x requires it). A free Apify account, which you can create with an email address or a GitHub login. Your API token, from Settings > API & Integrations in Apify Console. Install the client and export the token: pip install -U "apify-client~=3.0" export APIFY_API_TOKEN="your_apify_token_here" No scraping code is needed on your side. The Actor does the fetching. What you'll achieve You will search funda.nl for rentals in Utrecht up to 1,500 EUR per month, read the rows in Python and print a one-line summary per listing, including a price per square metre that you work out yourself from two fields. Funda lists more than homes, so a rental search also returns parking spaces and storage units. You will see how to spot them and how to filter them out. The same script works for a buyer comparing asking prices across towns, a tenant watching new rentals, or an analyst building a table of energy labels by neighbourhood. Only the input changes. Step 1: Open Funda Scraper Open the Funda Scraper page on Apify Store. The Try for free button there opens the Actor in Apify Console. This tutorial uses the API from Python, so you only need the Actor name, reventadata/funda-scraper. Step 2: Choose the search The search is described by a handful of input fields: offering: sale or rent. Anything else is refused before the run starts. areas: a list of Funda area slugs such as amsterdam or utrecht, copied from the selected_area part of a funda.nl search URL. Each area is one search, and a listing found twice is kept once. Leave the list empty and the Actor searches the whole Netherlands. objectType: empty (every type), house or apartment. sort: relevance (Funda's default) or newest. maxPrice and minPrice: in EUR, and for rentals per month. minLivingAreaM2, maxLivingAreaM2, minBedrooms: size filters. maxItems and maxPages: caps on rows and on pages per area. A search with a maxPrice sends the price range to Funda, so Funda does that filtering. The living-area and bedroom limits are applied by the Actor after it has read a page, so they remove rows but do not reduce the number of pages fetched. To search two towns for larger apartments for sale, the input would look like this: Step 3: Run it from Python This script starts the Actor, waits for it, reads the dataset and prints two lines per listing: import os from apify_client import ApifyClient # 1. Initialise the client with your token from the environment client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_API_TOKEN"]) # 2. Describe the search: rentals in Utrecht up to 1,500 EUR a month run_input = { "offering": "rent", "areas": ["utrecht"], "maxPrice": 1500, "maxItems": 15, "maxPages": 1, } # 3. Start the Actor and wait for it to finish run = client.actor("reventadata/funda-scraper").call(run_input=run_input) if run is None or run.status != "SUCCEEDED": status = run.status if run else "unknown" raise SystemExit(f"Run did not succeed (status: {status}).") # 4. Read the rows from the run's default dataset items = client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).list_items().items print(f"Retrieved {len(items)} listings.\n") # 5. Print two lines per listing, with a price per square metre worked out here for item in items: street = " ".join( part for part in (item.get("street"), item.get("houseNumber"), item.get("houseNumberSuffix")) if part ) price, area = item.get("price"), item.get("livingAreaM2") per_m2 = f"{price / area:.1f} EUR/m2" if price and area else "no living area" print(f"{street}, {item.get('city')} | {price} EUR/month | {area} m2 | {per_m2}") print(f" {item.get('propertyType')}, bedrooms: {item.get('bedrooms')}, energy label: {item.get('energyLabel')}") Fetching goes through an unblocking service, one page at a time, so keep maxPages small while you test. Step 4: Read the output The loop prints one block per listing. This is the start of its output on a capture dated 2026-11-07 (a Utrecht rental search with maxPrice 1,500, 15 rows on page 1): Koningsweg 135 E, Utrecht | 290 EUR/month | None m2 | no living area parking, bedrooms: None, energy label: unknown Hooft Graaflandstraat 2 A9, Utrecht | 1425 EUR/month | 27 m2 | 52.8 EUR/m2 apartment, bedrooms: 1, energy label: A++++ Oranje Vrijbuiterslaan 55, Utrecht | 1132 EUR/month | 48 m2 | 23.6 EUR/m2 The first listing is a parking space: no living area, no bedrooms. The Actor keeps it because objectType was left empty, and it reports the missing values as null rather than guessing. Step 5: Add coordinates and the description (optional) Set includeDetails to true and the Actor opens each kept listing's own page for latitude, longitude, the full Dutch description and the feature table. A listing whose page cannot be read still ships, with those four fields null. The detail fields look like this on a capture of one rental listing's page (description and features shortened): Understanding your results Every row carries 38 fields. The ones you will use most: price, priceCondition, priceType: the amount, and how Funda labels it (per_month for rent, kosten_koper for sale). street, houseNumber, houseNumberSuffix, postalCode, city, district, neighbourhood: the address, split up. livingAreaM2, plotAreaM2, rooms, bedrooms, energyLabel: size and energy label, as published. An unlabelled home shows "unknown". agencyName, agencyUrl, agencyAssociation, brokerName: the listing agency, and the broker when the listing names one. imageUrls, publishedAt, openHouses, promoText: photos, publication time, open-house windows, promo line. One complete row from the same capture (imageUrls cut to its first entry): The last four fields are null without details. Pro tips Filter by type early. In that capture 5 of 15 rows were parking spaces or storage. Set objectType to apartment or house to leave them out. Use newest for monitoring. sort: "newest" puts fresh listings first, which suits a schedule that checks for new homes. minPrice alone filters after the fetch. It is only sent to Funda together with maxPrice, so by itself it removes rows but does not save pages. Add includeDetails only when you need it. See Step 5: it costs one extra request per row. Compute your own ratios. There is no price-per-square-metre field. Divide price by livingAreaM2 yourself, as the script does, and skip rows where either is null. Mind the ceiling. Funda serves at most 666 pages of 15 results (9,990) for any one search. If a search is larger, the run logs a warning; narrow it with a price range, a type or a smaller area. Troubleshooting Zero rows, status SUCCEEDED. The site answered but nothing matched, or the area slug is unknown. The status message says so. Check the spelling against a funda.nl URL. Zero rows, status FAILED. A malformed slug or a maxPrice below minPrice ends the run with a message to fix the input. Pages that could not be read also fail a run that saved nothing. Fewer rows than expected. The log ends with Skipped N: reason lines for rows removed by your limits, and Pushed N row(s).. Read it with client.log(run.id).get(). Funda's terms of use restrict automated collection, so check that your use of the data complies with them and with data-protection law. Next steps For current pricing and details, see the Store page. To repeat a search, save it as an Apify task and attach a schedule, which runs an Actor or task on a cron expression. Datasets export as JSON, CSV, XML, Excel, HTML table, RSS or JSONL (dataset docs), and a webhook can call your own endpoint when a run finishes (webhook docs). What are you planning to search for on Funda? Drop a comment! 💬 About the author: reventadata builds and publishes data extraction Actors on the Apify Store.

articles.title: How to Scrape Immobiliare.it Listings with Python and Apify
articles.description: By the end of this tutorial you will have a Python script that pulls Italian property listings from Immobiliare.it into structured Python dictionaries: asking price or monthly rent in euros, surface area in square metres, rooms, floor, coordinates, feature tags, and the agency and agent contact details published on the ad. We use the Apify Actor Immobiliare.it Scraper (reventadata/immobiliare-scraper) and the official Apify Python client, so you do not need to run a browser, configure proxies, or parse HTML yourself. If you are looking for a practical way to scrape Immobiliare.it across cities, provinces, or regions, this guide walks through configuring a rental search in Torino, inspecting the returned fields, and ranking rentals by monthly rent per square metre. ⏱️ Time estimate: Setup takes a few minutes. This Actor is unofficial and not affiliated with Immobiliare.it. Prerequisites You need three things before running the script: Python 3.11 or newer (apify-client 3.x requires Python 3.11+). A free Apify account and your personal API token from the API & Integrations page in Apify Console. The official Apify Python client library installed in your environment: pip install -U "apify-client~=3.0" Export your API token in your shell so it stays out of your source code: export APIFY_API_TOKEN="your_apify_token_here" What you'll achieve You will run Immobiliare.it Scraper from Python and receive one dictionary per property ad, ready to filter in Python or export as JSON, CSV, or Excel. Each record includes numeric and formatted prices, price reduction details when a listing has been discounted, room and bathroom counts, numeric floor area in square metres (surfaceM2), street address, neighbourhood, city, province, region, latitude and longitude, photo URLs, and public seller contact fields (agencyName, agencyPhone, agentName, agentPhone). As a concrete example, we will search Torino rentals between 500 and 900 EUR per month with at least two rooms, then rank sample rows by monthly rent per square metre (price / surfaceM2) to spot the lowest cost per square metre. Step 1: Open the Actor Go to the Immobiliare.it Scraper page on Apify Store to review the input schema and documentation. Because we trigger the run from Python, you do not need to fill in the web form. Step 2: Configure the search parameters The Actor accepts the following input fields, sending your filter parameters directly in the immobiliare.it search URL: Field Type Default What it does contract string "sale" "sale" (vendita-case) or "rent" (affitto-case). location "torino" Location slug from an Immobiliare.it search URL, such as "torino", "milano", "torino-provincia", or "lombardia". minPrice, maxPrice integer unset Optional price limits in EUR (prezzoMinimo, prezzoMassimo). On rent searches this is the monthly rent. minSurface Optional minimum surface in m² (superficieMinima). minRooms, maxRooms Optional room (locali) limits (localiMinimo, localiMassimo). sortBy "relevance" "relevance" (site default) or "priceAscending" (criterio=prezzo&ordine=asc). maxItems 1000 Maximum number of rows pushed to the dataset. maxPages 80 Maximum result pages fetched (25 ads per page), capped at the site ceiling of 80. Both contract and sortBy are enum fields in the input schema: any value outside their allowed choices is refused before the run starts. To find a location slug, run a search on immobiliare.it and copy the path segment after /vendita-case/ or /affitto-case/. Here is the first part of our Python script, defining a rental search in Torino between 500 and 900 EUR per month with at least 2 rooms: import os from apify_client import ApifyClient # 1. Initialize the client with your token from the environment client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_API_TOKEN"]) # 2. Describe the search: rent in Torino, 500 to 900 EUR/month, at least 2 rooms run_input = { "contract": "rent", "location": "torino", "minPrice": 500, "maxPrice": 900, "minRooms": 2, "sortBy": "relevance", "maxItems": 20, "maxPages": 1, } Step 3: Run the Actor Call the Actor with client.actor("reventadata/immobiliare-scraper").call(run_input=run_input). It starts the run on Apify, waits for completion, and returns the settled run object: # 3. Start the Actor and wait for it to finish run = client.actor("reventadata/immobiliare-scraper").call(run_input=run_input) if run is None or run.status != "SUCCEEDED": status = run.status if run else "unknown" raise SystemExit(f"Run did not succeed (status: {status}).") # 4. Read the rows from the run's default dataset items = client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).list_items().items print(f"Retrieved {len(items)} listings.") articles.title: How to Scrape German Real Estate Listings with ImmoScout24 Scraper
articles.description: By the end of this tutorial you will have a Python script that turns an ImmoScout24 search, for example Berlin apartments to rent under 1,500 EUR, into structured rows: price, living space, rooms, address, coordinates, the agent behind the listing and the phone number they published. ImmoScout24 (immobilienscout24.de) is a German real-estate portal. Copying listings by hand does not scale: a capture of the Berlin rent search dated 2026-11-07 reports 13,833 hits spread over 662 result pages. While building this Actor I also sent 25 search-page requests from a plain Python HTTP client on 2026-11-07, and all 25 came back as the site's "Ich bin kein Roboter" check page. The Apify Actor ImmoScout24 Scraper (reventadata/immobilienscout24-scraper) does the page reading for you, and you call it from Python. Unofficial. This Actor is not affiliated with, endorsed by or connected to ImmoScout24 or Scout24. Prerequisites You need Python 3.11 or newer (apify-client 3.x requires it), an Apify account and an API token from API & Integrations in Apify Console. Install the client: pip install -U "apify-client~=3.0" Put the token in an environment variable so it never lands in your code: export APIFY_API_TOKEN="your_apify_token_here" What you'll achieve You will run one search, rent or buy, apartment or house, for one German city, and get one dataset row per listing. Each row carries the price, living space, rooms, postal address, coordinates when the seller shows the exact address, energy class, feature tags, photo links and the agent's company, contact name and phone. The result is a dataset you can export or read through the API, one row per listing, with the same field names every time. Example use case: you are looking at Berlin apartments to rent with at most 1,500 EUR base rent and at least 50 m², and you want them ranked by rent per square metre. The last step does exactly that. Step 1: Open the Actor Open the ImmoScout24 Scraper page on Apify Store. It lists the input fields and the output. This tutorial drives the Actor from Python, so you only need its name: reventadata/immobilienscout24-scraper. Step 2: Configure the search There are two ways to describe a search. A place. Fill state and city with the slugs from an ImmoScout24 address (berlin and berlin, bayern and muenchen, hessen and frankfurt-am-main), then pick listingType (rent or buy) and propertyType (apartment or house). A value outside those lists is refused before the run starts. A pasted URL. Put an ImmoScout24 search address in startUrls. Supported are /Suche/de/// followed by wohnung-mieten, wohnung-kaufen or haus-kaufen, with the price, livingspace, numberofrooms and sorting filters the site writes into the address. Here is the first way, with numeric limits: import os from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_API_TOKEN"]) run_input = { "state": "berlin", "city": "berlin", "listingType": "rent", "propertyType": "apartment", "maxPrice": 1500, "minLivingSpaceM2": 50, "includeGroupedListings": False, "maxItems": 50, "maxPages": 3, } maxPrice and minLivingSpaceM2 are applied by the Actor after a page is fetched, and a listing that lacks the value is dropped. maxItems caps the rows saved, and maxPages caps the result pages walked per search. Step 3: Optional settings The second way hands the filtering to the site itself, which is the better choice when you have already built the search in your browser: "startUrls": [ {"url": "https://www.immobilienscout24.de/Suche/de/berlin/berlin/wohnung-mieten?price=1000.0-1500.0&livingspace=50.0-80.0"} ], "maxPages": 2, includeGroupedListings is on by default. The site folds the other units of a new-build project under one card; the Actor saves them as separate rows with groupedUnderId set. Setting it to False, as in both snippets, keeps only the cards. Step 4: Run it and read the rows Call the Actor and read the dataset. call() waits until the run ends. run = client.actor("reventadata/immobilienscout24-scraper").call(run_input=run_input) if run is None or run.status != "SUCCEEDED": status = run.status if run else "unknown" raise SystemExit(f"Run did not succeed (status: {status}).") items = client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).list_items().items print(f"Retrieved {len(items)} listings.\n") Then print what you got: for item in items: size = f'{item.get("livingSpaceM2")} m²' if item.get("livingSpaceM2") else "size not stated" print(f'{item.get("price")} {item.get("currency")} | {size} | {item.get("rooms")} rooms | {item.get("postcode")} {item.get("quarter")}') print(f' {item.get("title")}') print(f' {item.get("url")}') phone = item.get("contactPhone") or item.get("contactMobile") or "no phone published" print(f' {item.get("realtorCompanyName") or "no company shown"} | {phone}') Here is one row from the sample rows from a run on 2026-11-10 (Hamburg apartments to rent, minRooms: 2, maxPrice: 1500), with the photos list shortened to two entries: Understanding your results price is the base rent per month on rent searches (priceInterval is MONTH) and the purchase price on buy searches. totalRent is the calculated total rent when the site shows one; the sample row has both. livingSpaceM2, rooms and, for houses, plotAreaM2 are numbers. Yes/no fields such as hasBalcony, hasLift or hasCellar are null when the listing does not say, not false. latitude and longitude come with the exact address. In the capture, 19 of the 20 cards carry coordinates. contactPhone and contactMobile are the numbers the seller published in the results list. In the capture, 8 of the 20 cards carry one. The Actor does not open listing pages. groupedUnderId is null for a card and holds the card's id for a unit folded under it. photos are links filled in at 800x600. realtorCompanyName, contactFirstName and contactLastName name the agent and the contact the listing shows. url opens the listing on the site. Pro tips Mind the grouped units. Page 1 of that capture holds 20 cards and 205 grouped units, so 225 rows for one page if you leave includeGroupedListings on. Filter on the site when you can. A URL filter shrinks what is fetched; minPrice, maxPrice, minLivingSpaceM2, maxLivingSpaceM2, minRooms and maxRooms only drop rows afterwards. Start small. maxItems defaults to 100 and maxPages to 50. The input description warns that a page can take 15 to 45 seconds, so try maxPages: 1 first. Rank your own way. This reads the rows from the run above and sorts by rent per square metre: priced = [i for i in items if i.get("price") and i.get("livingSpaceM2")] for i in priced[:5]: print(f'{i["price"] / i["livingSpaceM2"]:.1f} EUR/m² | {i["url"]}') Ids are unique. A listing that moves between pages while the run walks is saved once. Mind the caps. Both maxItems and maxPages stop the run, whichever limit is reached first. Troubleshooting Zero rows. If the site answers but nothing matches (or your limits drop everything), the run ends SUCCEEDED with a status message and an empty dataset. If pages could not be read and no row was saved, the run is marked FAILED with the reason. Unknown city slug. With no rows saved, the run ends FAILED with a slug message (after earlier rows, it logs a warning). Copy both slugs from a search address. Houses for rent. The input allows rent with house, but the Actor stops with a message: only apartments for rent, apartments for sale and houses for sale are offered. A price of 0. In the capture, 2 of the 29 rows on the Berlin houses-for-sale page 2 carry a price of 0 in the site's data and the Actor passes it on. Set minPrice to 1 to drop such rows. Pricing and Next Steps For current pricing and details, see the Store page. To repeat a search automatically, save it as a task and attach an Apify schedule, which starts an Actor on a cron expression. The Apify Python client docs cover the rest of the API. What would you track on ImmoScout24: rents in one city, houses for sale, or an agent's listings? Drop a comment below.
